title: Ancient DNA Links Ice Age Europeans Across the Continent
paragraphs: Few periods feel as remote as the Ice Age, yet a study in Science Advances, led by the University of Vienna and signed by 37 authors, suggests that its inhabitants were more closely connected than once believed. The work centres on the Gravettian culture, which stretched across Europe from roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago.

At its heart lies the genome of a woman who lived some 30,000 years ago in Isturitz Cave, in France, the oldest genome-wide dataset from a modern human in southwestern Europe. Though her ancestry was predominantly western, she also carried central and eastern European strands, and modelling places the mixing between about 32,500 and 31,500 years ago. “Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed,” said lead author Pere Gelabert.

The team also recovered DNA from sediment in a 22,000-year-old layer at El Mirón Cave, in northern Spain, where no human bones or teeth survive; the authors read this as support for the Iberian Peninsula serving as a refuge through the coldest stretch of the Ice Age. A few caveats are in order. The central result hinges on a single individual, several readings are phrased as probable rather than proven, and the press release names no funding. It is a tantalising glimpse, not the final word.

questions.q: What does the Isturitz woman’s ancestry suggest?
questions.a: That eastern and western groups were in contact and mixed.

questions.q: What is unusual about the El Mirón evidence?
questions.a: The DNA came from sediment, with no human bones or teeth present.

questions.q: What does “not the final word” imply?
questions.a: The conclusions may still change with more evidence.
